Prioritise one visible vertical alignment in the middle of the picture: black nozzle above, fine drops in the air, and slightly damp compost touching the base of the beetroot below. The centre of the nozzle opening and the crown that receives the watering should be at almost exactly the same horizontal position in the finished image. Design the entire composition around that relationship.

Use the physical camera truth from the first photograph: John's real low timber bed, ordinary lawn and square slabs on the right, horizontal brown shed siding behind him at the right only, the old split wood stacked behind the bed and deep green hedge. Preserve that perspective viewed from the same side of the bed, slightly closer to the watering. John stands off the bed on the grass at the right. Crop him from his chest to upper legs, head outside the frame. His actual checked shirt sleeves and ordinary grip with both bare hands. Reproduce his actual medium-sized blue moulded watering can with a single arch handle, one slim tapered spout and the small dark rose as seen in the photograph. One hand holds the upper handle and the other supports the can's rear, two hands attached to plausible forearms. The can is raised and extended over the crop, just above it, normal size. The rose hangs directly above the selected central beetroot's soil line. Keep the whole blue can, rose and the central crown visible in the image, no extra tools or altered buildings.

Choose the nearby beetroot planted at the centre of the scene so its low stem base can be seen on dark crumbly compost. Let its foliage naturally splay to either side slightly, leaving a small line of sight to soil at the stem base. Direct the rose face nearly down. A small clear shower of sparse separate fine drops falls quite vertically onto the same plant's immediate rooting area, within a finger's width of that visible stem base on the side closer to the camera. Water lands as a small dark damp patch touching the plant base, soaking in, no standing puddles, no high pressure or heavy splash. Short range, straight down. It should be unmistakably aimed at soil at this specific beetroot. A couple of leaves out of the way, no wide bare gap between stem and water.

Copy how leaves in the actual beetroot reference bend and turn sideways, with varied leaf sizes and red-purple veins, curled and overlapping stalks, an occasional faded or slightly nibbled lower leaf and some more compact plants behind. Crop is in a few roughly spaced clumps with open compost between them. Roots sit down in the earth, show at most a small uneven top shoulder at soil level beneath the red stem bases, no exposed displayed spheres. Soft near-green and red-purple tones, ordinary slightly weathered bed and no repeating rosettes. A fresh unposed camera frame from an established garden, believable natural directional daylight, a bit quieter than a commercial garden photograph. Everything physically coherent and legible when the image is 90mm wide, no labels, no border.
